3.   Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract or other legal act under Union or Member State law, that is binding on the processor with regard to the controller and that sets out the subject-matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects and the obligations and rights of the controller. That contract or other legal act shall stipulate, in particular, that the processor:

(a)

processes the personal data only on documented instructions from the controller, including with regard to transfers of personal data to a third country or an international organisation, unless required to do so by Union or Member State law to which the processor is subject; in such a case, the processor shall inform the controller of that legal requirement before processing, unless that law prohibits such information on important grounds of public interest;

(b)

ensures that persons authorised to process the personal data have committed themselves to confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality;

(c)

takes all measures required pursuant to Article 32;

(d)

respects the conditions referred to in paragraphs 2 and 4 for engaging another processor;

(e)

taking into account the nature of the processing, assists the controller by appropriate technical and organisational measures, insofar as this is possible, for the fulfilment of the controller's obligation to respond to requests for exercising the data subject's rights laid down in Chapter III;

(f)

assists the controller in ensuring compliance with the obligations pursuant to Articles 32 to 36 taking into account the nature of processing and the information available to the processor;

(g)

at the choice of the controller, deletes or returns all the personal data to the controller after the end of the provision of services relating to processing, and deletes existing copies unless Union or Member State law requires storage of the personal data;

(h)

makes available to the controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance with the obligations laid down in this Article and allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the controller or another auditor mandated by the controller.

4.   Where a processor engages another processor for carrying out specific processing activities on behalf of the controller, the same data protection obligations as set out in the contract or other legal act between the controller and the processor as referred to in paragraph 3 shall be imposed on that other processor by way of a contract or other legal act under Union or Member State law, in particular providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in such a manner that the processing will meet the requirements of this Regulation. Where that other processor fails to fulfil its data protection obligations, the initial processor shall remain fully liable to the controller for the performance of that other processor's obligations.

Such powers should also include the power to impose a temporary or definitive limitation, including a ban, on processing. Member States may specify other tasks related to the protection of personal data under this Regulation. The powers of supervisory authorities should be exercised in accordance with appropriate procedural safeguards set out in Union and Member State law, impartially, fairly and within a reasonable time. In particular each measure should be appropriate, necessary and proportionate in view of ensuring compliance with this Regulation, taking into account the circumstances of each individual case, respect the right of every person to be heard before any individual measure which would affect him or her adversely is taken and avoid superfluous costs and excessive inconveniences for the persons concerned. Investigatory powers as regards access to premises should be exercised in accordance with specific requirements in Member State procedural law, such as the requirement to obtain a prior judicial authorisation. Each legally binding measure of the supervisory authority should be in writing, be clear and unambiguous, indicate the supervisory authority which has issued the measure, the date of issue of the measure, bear the signature of the head, or a member of the supervisory authority authorised by him or her, give the reasons for the measure, and refer to the right of an effective remedy. This should not preclude additional requirements pursuant to Member State procedural law. The adoption of a legally binding decision implies that it may give rise to judicial review in the Member State of the supervisory authority that adopted the decision.

(130)

In such cases, the lead supervisory authority should, when taking measures intended to produce legal effects, including the imposition of administrative fines, take utmost account of the view of the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged and which should remain competent to carry out any investigation on the territory of its own Member State in liaison with the competent supervisory authority.

(132)

Where a competent authority for the registration of data altruism organisations in one Member State requests assistance from a competent authority for the registration of data altruism organisations in another Member State, it shall submit a reasoned request. European data altruism consent form

1.   In order to facilitate the collection of data based on data altruism, the Commission shall adopt implementing acts establishing and developing a European data altruism consent form, after consulting the European Data Protection Board, taking into account the advice of the European Data Innovation Board and duly involving relevant stakeholders. 3.   Where personal data are provided, the European data altruism consent form shall ensure that data subjects are able to give consent to and withdraw consent from a specific data processing operation in compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

4.   The form shall be available in a manner that can be printed on paper and is easily understandable as well as in an electronic, machine-readable form.

Competent authorities and procedural provisions

Article 26

Requirements relating to competent authorities

1.   The competent authorities for data intermediation services and the competent authorities for the registration of data altruism organisations shall be legally distinct from, and functionally independent of, any data intermediation services provider or recognised data altruism organisation. entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.

entity: "MEMBER STATE" | type: "PARTY" | description: A Member State is defined as a sovereign country that is a part of the European Union (EU), thereby subject to its laws and regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation 2016/679). entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.

entity: "DATA HOLDERS" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Data Holders" refer to individuals or entities that possess, control, or manage data, with the capacity to make that data available for processing. entity: "REGULATION" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "The Regulation sets out the legal framework for the processing and protection of personal data within the European Union."<SEP>REGULATION refers to a comprehensive legal framework established within the European Union to govern the use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and manage the handling, sharing, and processing of data, with a strong emphasis on the protection of individuals' rights. One key aspect of the REGULATION is its determination of the responsibilities and obligations of providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, as well as those associated with general-purpose AI models. It sets forth guidelines for the classification and assessment of these AI systems, requiring compliance with safety standards and prohibiting manipulative practices, especially in contexts involving biometric data. Additionally, the REGULATION outlines rules to ensure non-discriminatory application and protection of individuals' rights across the Union.

The REGULATION also establishes mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement of AI systems, detailing the functioning of supportive bodies such as advisory forums and scientific panels. It specifies the legal framework for the management of biometric identification systems, including their usage and implications for privacy. The REGULATION encompasses a range of aspects including standardization processes, provisions for interoperability, and the roles and responsibilities of data holders and users of connected products.

Moreover, it aims to facilitate smooth transitions between data processing services, allowing users to efficiently transfer their data and digital assets while ensuring that data access and usage are governed by consent or legitimate interest. It specifies the obligations of data holders and includes provisions for resolving disputes related to data handling, ensuring fairness in contractual arrangements.

question: What is the European Data Innovation Board?
ground_truth: As per Article 29(1), the European Data Innovation Board is an expert group set up by the Commission and constituted by representatives from Member States' competent authorities for data intermediation services and data altruism, EU data protection bodies, ENISA, the Commission itself, SME envoys, and other sector specific or expert organizations. The Commission will chair the meetings of the Board (Article 29(3)). As per Article 29(2), the Board will be structured into three subgroups: (A) A subgroup composed of competent authorities for data intermediation services and registration of data altruism organisations; (B) A subgroup for technical discussions on standardisation, portability and interoperability; (C) A subgroup for stakeholder involvement. As per Article 30, the Board is tasked with various prerogatives including: overseeing the activities of data intermediaries and data altruism organisations; coordinating and advising on data governance and implementation of the DGA at the EU level; and advising the Commission on matters of standardisation and interoperability.
answer:
The **European Data Innovation Board (EDIB)** is a pivotal organization within the European Union's framework dedicated to enhancing data governance and promoting data intermediation services. Established primarily under the auspices of the European Commission, the EDIB serves multiple functions related to data management, strategic guidance, and compliance within the EU context.

### Overview and Purpose

The EDIB functions as an expert group composed of representatives from various competent authorities involved in data intermediation and altruism across all Member States. Its formation aims to foster cooperation and establish a consistent practice for handling data requests, guiding public sector bodies, and supporting the implementation of effective data altruism initiatives. 

One significant responsibility of the EDIB is to provide recommendations to Member States regarding the penalties and compliance measures related to data intermediation services. The advisory role it plays is critical in shaping best practices that govern data sharing and ensures that these practices align with broader EU regulations, notably the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Data Governance Act.

### Key Functions

1. **Advisory Role**: The EDIB assists the European Commission in developing standards and recommendations for the implementation of data governance laws. This includes establishing consistent criteria for data intermediation services across member states.

2. **Guidance on Data Altruism**: The organization contributes to frameworks that promote data altruism–the act of sharing data for the common good without financial benefit. This is vital for ensuring that data collective initiatives are conducted responsibly.

3. **Facilitating Cooperation Among Member States**: The EDIB plays a key role in harmonizing practices across different nations, ensuring that all Member States adhere to shared standards regarding data management and protection.

4. **Supporting Technological Innovation**: By acting as a bridge between different authorities and stakeholders, the EDIB also helps identify and promote technology that drives innovation in data handling and processing.

### Relationship with Other Entities

The European Data Innovation Board is closely associated with the **European Data Protection Board (EDPB)**, which oversees data protection compliance strategies across the Union. Moreover, the EDIB collaborates with **Member States**, **the European Commission**, and various **competent authorities** to streamline data governance inclusive of innovative solutions that prioritize individual rights and data privacy.

As such, the EDIB's activities and recommendations not only empower Member States to better manage data-related tasks but also reinforce the overall EU goal of establishing a coherent and effective data economy that respects and protects the data rights of individuals.

### Conclusion

The European Data Innovation Board embodies a collaborative effort to uphold high data protection standards, facilitate responsible data sharing, and ensure that data governance in Europe evolves alongside technological advancements. Its strategic significance is underscored by its role in harmonizing regulations, advising on compliance, and promoting innovation in data management. In a rapidly changing digital landscape, the EDIB is fundamental in shaping a future-oriented data governance framework that respects the rights of data subjects while fostering technological progress across the EU.

Right to lodge a complaint

1.   Natural and legal persons shall have the right to lodge a complaint in relation to any matter falling within the scope of this Regulation, individually or, where relevant, collectively, with the relevant competent authority for data intermediation services against a data intermediation services provider or with the relevant competent authority for the registration of data altruism organisations against a recognised data altruism organisation.

Article 28

Right to an effective judicial remedy

1.   Notwithstanding any administrative or other non-judicial remedies, any affected natural and legal persons shall have the right to an effective judicial remedy with regard to legally binding decisions referred to in Article 14 taken by the competent authorities for data intermediation services in the management, control and enforcement of the notification regime for data intermediation services providers and legally binding decisions referred to in Articles 19 and 24 taken by the competent authorities for the registration of data altruism organisations in the monitoring of recognised data altruism organisations.

European Data Innovation Board

Article 29

European Data Innovation Board

1.   The Commission shall establish a European Data Innovation Board in the form of an expert group, consisting of representatives of the competent authorities for data intermediation services and the competent authorities for the registration of data altruism organisations of all Member States, the European Data Protection Board, the European Data Protection Supervisor, ENISA, the Commission, the EU SME Envoy or a representative appointed by the network of SME envoys, and other representatives of relevant bodies in specific sectors as well as bodies with specific expertise. In its appointments of individual experts, the Commission shall aim to achieve gender and geographical balance among the members of the expert group.

2.   The European Data Innovation Board shall consist of at least the following three subgroups:

(a)

Those notions may vary with regard to the relevant context and can include understanding the correct application of technical elements during the AI system’s development phase, the measures to be applied during its use, the suitable ways in which to interpret the AI system’s output, and, in the case of affected persons, the knowledge necessary to understand how decisions taken with the assistance of AI will have an impact on them. In the context of the application this Regulation, AI literacy should provide all relevant actors in the AI value chain with the insights required to ensure the appropriate compliance and its correct enforcement. Furthermore, the wide implementation of AI literacy measures and the introduction of appropriate follow-up actions could contribute to improving working conditions and ultimately sustain the consolidation, and innovation path of trustworthy AI in the Union. The European Artificial Intelligence Board (the ‘Board’) should support the Commission, to promote AI literacy tools, public awareness and understanding of the benefits, risks, safeguards, rights and obligations in relation to the use of AI systems. In cooperation with the relevant stakeholders, the Commission and the Member States should facilitate the drawing up of voluntary codes of conduct to advance AI literacy among persons dealing with the development, operation and use of AI.

(21)

In order to ensure a level playing field and an effective protection of rights and freedoms of individuals across the Union, the rules established by this Regulation should apply to providers of AI systems in a non-discriminatory manner, irrespective of whether they are established within the Union or in a third country, and to deployers of AI systems established within the Union.

(22)

In light of their digital nature, certain AI systems should fall within the scope of this Regulation even when they are not placed on the market, put into service, or used in the Union. This is the case, for example, where an operator established in the Union contracts certain services to an operator established in a third country in relation to an activity to be performed by an AI system that would qualify as high-risk. In those circumstances, the AI system used in a third country by the operator could process data lawfully collected in and transferred from the Union, and provide to the contracting operator in the Union the output of that AI system resulting from that processing, without that AI system being placed on the market, put into service or used in the Union. To prevent the circumvention of this Regulation and to ensure an effective protection of natural persons located in the Union, this Regulation should also apply to providers and deployers of AI systems that are established in a third country, to the extent the output produced by those systems is intended to be used in the Union. Nonetheless, to take into account existing arrangements and special needs for future cooperation with foreign partners with whom information and evidence is exchanged, this Regulation should not apply to public authorities of a third country and international organisations when acting in the framework of cooperation or international agreements concluded at Union or national level for law enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union or the Member States, provided that the relevant third country or international organisation provides adequate safeguards with respect to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. ground_truth: As per Article 1(1), the Data Act establishes rules on a set of diverse topics that exhaustively include: (a) The making available of product data and related service data to users of connected products or related services; (b) The making available of data by data holders to data recipients; (c) The making available of data by data holders to public sector bodies, the European Commission, the European Central Bank and Union bodies in case of an exceptional need for those data for the performance of a specific task carried out in the public interest; (d) The facilitation of switching between data processing services; (e) The introduction of safeguards against unlawful third-party access to non-personal data; (f) The development of interoperability standards for accessing, transferring and use of data.

## Overview of the Data Act

The **Data Act** is a significant legislative framework established within the **European Union** aimed at promoting fair access to and use of data across various sectors. Enacted under the broader objectives of fostering data sharing and ensuring compliance with established regulations, the Data Act addresses both personal and non-personal data. It underscores the importance of transparency and ethical use of data to enhance innovation and collaboration among stakeholders.

### Key Objectives of the Data Act

1. **Facilitating Data Sharing**: 
   The Data Act establishes rules that encourage data sharing among various entities, including private companies, public sector bodies, and data holders. It promotes the voluntary sharing of data for public good, highlighting the principle of **data altruism**. This aspect is crucial for enabling collaborative efforts in addressing societal challenges such as healthcare, climate change, and scientific research.

2. **Regulatory Compliance**:
   Compliance with legal obligations is a central tenet of the Data Act. It sets forth requirements that data holders and users must meet, ensuring that all data sharing adheres to relevant regulations, particularly concerning data protection laws like the **GDPR** (General Data Protection Regulation).

3. **Ensuring Transparency**:
   The Data Act mandates transparency in data practices, requiring data holders to communicate clearly about how data will be shared, used, and processed. This obligation aims to foster trust among data subjects and stakeholders involved in the data ecosystem.

### Key Provisions

- **Conditions for Data Re-use**: The Act specifies conditions under which data can be reused by public sector bodies and other stakeholders, ensuring that any data access is non-discriminatory and follows clear guidelines.
  
- **Transparency Obligations**: Entities handling data are required to disclose comprehensive information about their processing activities to uphold accountability and inform data subjects about their rights.

- **Public Interest Considerations**: The Data Act recognizes the public interest as a foundational principle that might justify specific data processing operations without obtaining prior consent in certain contexts, particularly those contributing to societal well-being.

### Conclusion

In summary, the Data Act stands as a pivotal regulation within the EU's legislative framework, designed to streamline data access and reuse while ensuring compliance, transparency, and ethical standards in data management. By fostering an environment conducive to data sharing, the Data Act aims to harness the full potential of data for collective benefit while protecting the rights of individuals.

It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.
entity: "DATA HOLDER" | type: "PARTY" | description: A Data Holder is defined as an individual or entity that possesses or has control over data. They bear the responsibility for ensuring fair and legal use of this data in accordance with applicable regulations. Typically, a Data Holder can apply technical protection measures to prevent unauthorized access or disclosure of the data under their control. This role encompasses various obligations regarding both personal and non-personal data, requiring them to ensure data availability to users and third parties while maintaining compliance with legal mandates.

Data Holders manage and control access to the data they possess, ensuring its accuracy and confidentiality. They are legally entitled to grant access to or share the data they hold, including data generated from connected products or services, making them pivotal in data management. This includes responding to requests for data from public sector bodies and compliance with data access rights as stipulated by regulations.

As entities, Data Holders are subject to legal requirements related to data transparency, sharing, and confidentiality. They may engage in negotiations regarding data availability and often face obligations to share information in cases involving compensation calculations. Additionally, Data Holders are essential in managing trade secrets and must uphold various obligations surrounding data protection and sharing. 

In summary, a Data Holder plays a critical role in controlling, protecting, and managing access to data, while ensuring adherence to applicable legal and regulatory frameworks.
entity: "MEMBER STATES" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Member States are countries that are part of the European Union and work towards consistent data protection laws."<SEP>"Member States are countries within the EU that must adhere to the GDPR and its regulations concerning data protection and transfers."<SEP>"Member States are entities that are required to take necessary measures to comply with the Commission's decision regarding data protection."<SEP>"Member States refer to the individual countries in the EU that have obligations to inform the Commission regarding data flow regulations."<SEP>"Member States refers to the countries within the European Union that are governed by GDPR regulations and their interpretations."<SEP>Member States are the individual countries that comprise the European Union (EU) and are accountable for implementing and enforcing EU regulations, including those related to data protection, artificial intelligence (AI), and other pertinent directives. These Member States are responsible for enacting national legislation that aligns with EU laws while ensuring compliance within their jurisdictions.

Specifically, Member States have a legal obligation to implement Union law, including data protection regulations, and must establish their own supervisory authorities to oversee compliance. They are tasked with certifying dispute settlement bodies, enforcing data protection measures, and designating market surveillance authorities. In matters concerning AI, Member States are required to establish regulatory frameworks that include the implementation of AI systems regulations, particularly for high-risk applications, and must facilitate the registration and use of these systems.

Member States also play a crucial role in public security, defense, and national law, which allows them to influence how regulations are applied within their borders. They are required to notify the European Commission about their compliance measures, including rules on penalties for data transfer violations and guidelines for data processing. Additionally, they participate in discussions related to AI governance and are encouraged to support solutions that yield socially and environmentally beneficial outcomes.

Overall, Member States act as national authorities responsible for ensuring adherence to EU regulations while maintaining certain legislative competencies. They collaborate on law enforcement and judicial matters, engage in international agreements concerning data transfer, and are integral to the effective governance and oversight of both data protection and emerging technologies within the EU regulatory framework.<SEP>"Member States refer to the countries that are part of the European Union and subject to its data protection regulations."
entity: "DATA SUBJECTS" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Data Subjects are individuals whose personal data is being processed, entitled to rights and legal remedies under the GDPR."<SEP>"Data Subjects are individuals whose personal data is processed and who seek legal remedies against unlawful data practices."<SEP>"Data Subjects refer to individuals whose personal data is processed and who are entitled to certain rights under the GDPR."<SEP>"Data Subjects" are individuals whose personal data is collected and processed by various organizations, including data altruism organizations and data intermediation service providers. They are entitled to specific rights and protections under data protection regulations, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). These rights include access to their personal information, the ability to consent to data processing, and protections against unauthorized use of their data.

Data Subjects are recognized as natural persons whose data may be collected, shared, or processed, with particular attention given to ethical and legal standards governing their personal information. They possess rights related to their personal data, which are safeguarded by relevant laws and frameworks that ensure their privacy is maintained. Additionally, Data Subjects may find their data influenced by the practices of public sector bodies or other entities seeking consent for reuse.

In summary, Data Subjects are recognized not only for their role in the data ecosystem as those from whom data is collected, but also for the safeguards in place that aim to protect their rights and freedoms in the context of personal data processing.<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data may be processed within the context of AI systems and regulatory sandboxes."<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data are processed, and they hold rights concerning their data under GDPR and other regulations."<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is being processed and who have rights under the GDPR to protect their privacy and data."<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is being processed, and they are granted specific rights under GDPR to protect their data."<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is collected and processed, and they are central to the discussions of data protection."<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is processed, whose rights and interests must be protected under the GDPR."<SEP>"Data Subjects are individuals whose personal data is processed under the Regulation, thus having rights and protections defined by the Regulation."<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is processed and whose rights must be protected according to data protection regulations."<SEP>"Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is processed, having certain rights under the Regulation."
entity: "DATA SUBJECT" | type: "PARTY" | description: "A data subject is an individual whose personal data is being collected, held, or processed."<SEP>"The data subject is the individual whose non-personal data is being processed or accessed by data users, with specific rights regarding their data."<SEP>The term "Data Subject" refers to an identifiable natural person whose personal data is being processed. entity: "CONTROLLER" | type: "PARTY" | description: "A Controller is a person or entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data and has obligations under data protection laws."<SEP>The "Controller" is an entity, which can be either an individual or a legal person, responsible for determining the purposes and means of processing personal data. This entity holds significant legal responsibility for ensuring that all processing activities comply with relevant data protection regulations. As the primary decision-maker regarding personal data, the Controller must comply with data protection laws and bear liability for any damages caused by infringements during the processing of this data.

The Controller's duties include not only determining how and why personal data is processed but also following the directives of supervisory authorities overseeing data protection practices. They are obligated to ensure compliance with legal obligations concerning the handling and processing of personal data and play a critical role in safeguarding data protection standards.

In summary, the Controller is central to the accountability framework established by data protection regulations, serving as the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data while maintaining oversight and responsibility for compliance.<SEP>"A Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data, ensuring compliance with GDPR obligations."<SEP>"The Controller refers to the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data and is primarily responsible for data protection compliance and safeguards."<SEP>"The Controller refers to the individual or organization that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data under the GDPR."<SEP>"The controller is a natural or legal person or public authority that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data, significant in GDPR compliance."<SEP>"The controller is the entity responsible for determining the purposes and means of processing personal data, adhering to the obligations set forth in data protection regulations."<SEP>"A controller is an entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data, as defined within Regulation 2016/679."<SEP>"Controller is the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data and is responsible for compliance with the Regulation."<SEP>"The Controller is an entity or individual that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data under data protection laws."<SEP>"The controller is an entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data, relevant in the context of regulatory compliance."
entity: "GDPR" | type: "STATUTE" | description: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a comprehensive regulation in European Union (EU) law focused on data protection and privacy. It is designed to give individuals greater control over their personal data and establishes guidelines for the collection and processing of personal information within the EU. GDPR governs how personal data is handled, sets forth the responsibilities of data controllers and processors, and addresses the transfer of personal data outside the EU.

As a crucial legal framework, GDPR replaced the earlier Directive 95/46, reflecting advancements in technology and changes in societal expectations regarding privacy. It emphasizes the rights of individuals, including their right to access their data, rectify inaccuracies, and request deletion of their information. Overall, the GDPR aims to strengthen the protection of personal data and privacy for individuals within the European Union, making it one of the most significant pieces of legislation in the realm of data protection.
entity: "MEMBER STATE" | type: "PARTY" | description: A Member State is defined as a sovereign country that is a part of the European Union (EU), thereby subject to its laws and regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation 2016/679). Each Member State has its own supervisory authority responsible for enforcing data protection regulations and must comply with the GDPR and other EU regulations regarding data sharing, access, and protection. Member States are tasked with implementing regulatory frameworks that govern personal data usage, informing the European Commission about compliance issues, and designating competent authorities to ensure adherence to these regulations.

Additionally, Member States play a crucial role in the governance of data intermediation services and data altruism, supporting the responsible sharing and reuse of data for societal benefit, particularly by public sector bodies. They also bear significant responsibilities concerning high-risk AI systems and biometric identification systems, which include reporting their findings related to these areas to the Commission. Each Member State possesses its own market surveillance authorities and has the authority to enforce compliance through administrative fines.

In essence, Member States are key players within the EU framework, responsible not only for following but also for enforcing the Union's directives and regulations. They act as national entities that contribute to the overall governance and compliance of data protection policies, balancing regulatory adherence with the promotion of data altruism initiatives.

entity: "REGULATION (EU) 2016/679" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "Regulation (EU) 2016/679 is a key EU legislation concerning the protection of personal data and privacy for individuals."<SEP>"Regulation (EU) 2016/679 is the official title of the GDPR, which outlines the comprehensive framework for data protection within the European Union."<SEP>"Regulation (EU) 2016/679, also known as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), governs data protection and privacy within the European Union."<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2016/679, commonly known as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), is a comprehensive legislative framework established by the European Union that governs data protection and privacy for individuals within the EU and the European Economic Area. It came into effect on 27 April 2016 and aims to ensure the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects, with a particular emphasis on the protection of personal data.

The GDPR outlines specific rules for the collection and processing of personal information, emphasizing key principles such as consent and data portability. It delineates the responsibilities of data controllers, requiring them to handle personal data lawfully and setting out the legal bases for data processing. The regulation also addresses the balance between data protection and legitimate data usage, establishing guidelines that influence the operations of public sector bodies in managing data requests.

Moreover, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 impacts the use of AI technologies and mandates that monitoring authorities are established to ensure compliance with its provisions. As a cornerstone of the EU’s commitment to safeguarding individual rights and privacy in the digital age, the GDPR serves as a critical legal framework for personal data protection across member states.<SEP>"Regulation (EU) 2016/679 is the General Data Protection Regulation that governs data protection and privacy in the EU."<SEP>"Regulation (EU) 2016/679, also known as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), governs the processing of personal data in the EU."<SEP>"Regulation (EU) 2016/679 is the General Data Protection Regulation established by the European Parliament to protect natural persons concerning the processing of personal data."<SEP>"Regulation (EU) 2016/679, also known as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), is a comprehensive data protection law in the EU that governs the processing of personal data and aims to protect individual privacy rights."

entity: "REGULATION" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "The Regulation sets out the legal framework for the processing and protection of personal data within the European Union."<SEP>REGULATION refers to a comprehensive legal framework established within the European Union to govern the use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and manage the handling, sharing, and processing of data, with a strong emphasis on the protection of individuals' rights. It defines rules and directives that classify AI applications, particularly distinguishing high-risk AI systems and ensuring compliance with fundamental rights.

One key aspect of the REGULATION is its determination of the responsibilities and obligations of providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, as well as those associated with general-purpose AI models. It sets forth guidelines for the classification and assessment of these AI systems, requiring compliance with safety standards and prohibiting manipulative practices, especially in contexts involving biometric data. Additionally, the REGULATION outlines rules to ensure non-discriminatory application and protection of individuals' rights across the Union.

The REGULATION also establishes mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement of AI systems, detailing the functioning of supportive bodies such as advisory forums and scientific panels. It specifies the legal framework for the management of biometric identification systems, including their usage and implications for privacy. The REGULATION encompasses a range of aspects including standardization processes, provisions for interoperability, and the roles and responsibilities of data holders and users of connected products.

Moreover, it aims to facilitate smooth transitions between data processing services, allowing users to efficiently transfer their data and digital assets while ensuring that data access and usage are governed by consent or legitimate interest. It specifies the obligations of data holders and includes provisions for resolving disputes related to data handling, ensuring fairness in contractual arrangements. 

Overall, the REGULATION not only serves to protect individuals' rights—granting them access, rectification, and erasure of their personal data—but also demands consistency in the enforcement of data protection laws across Member States. By establishing these comprehensive guidelines and frameworks, the REGULATION promotes effective data management and enhances trust and security in data processing practices within the European Union.

entity: "DATA HOLDERS" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Data Holders" refer to individuals or entities that possess, control, or manage data, with the capacity to make that data available for processing. They may hold both personal and non-personal data, and their activities often comply with various regulations regarding data protection and sharing. 

Data Holders can share non-personal data under the principles of Data Altruism, aimed at achieving broader societal benefits. This sharing occurs with explicit consent from the Data Holders themselves, who grant permission for data processing by Data Altruism Organisations. In addition, these entities have specific rights over the data they hold, including the management of its use and protection.

The responsibilities of Data Holders include ensuring compliance with legal obligations when accessing, sharing, or exchanging data. Under new regulatory frameworks, they are mandated to share data with designated recipients. Furthermore, Data Holders are accountable for adhering to specific conditions set forth by law regarding access and usage, often involving the need to safeguard their interests and potentially receive compensation upon data sharing.

They may also be subject to requests for data access from public sector bodies or other authorities, highlighting their role in data transparency and the facilitation of data exchanges within the community, which may encompass both private and public sector organizations.

## Scope of Applicability of the Data Act

The Data Act, established by Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, sets forth a comprehensive legal framework aimed at promoting fair access to data and facilitating its use while preventing contractual imbalances between parties. Its reach is significant, addressing both personal and non-personal data in various contexts, particularly in the realm of public sector data management.

### Key Provisions of the Data Act

1. **Public Sector Data Utilization**:
   The Data Act encourages public sector bodies to make data available for use in a manner that aligns with the public interest. It delineates obligations regarding how datasets should be shared and accessed, ensuring that citizens and organizations have the opportunity to benefit from public data resources.

2. **Regulatory Framework for Data Sharing**:
   At the core of the Data Act is the establishment of rules that govern data sharing practices. These guidelines emphasize fair conditions for accessing and utilizing data while complying with legal obligations set forth by national and Union law. The Act is designed to create a balanced environment for both data holders and users, easing barriers that may exist in current data-sharing practices.

3. **Intermediation Services and User Rights**:
   The Data Act encompasses provisions concerning data intermediation services. These services facilitate commercial relationships between data holders and users while ensuring that individuals have control over their data. It mandates transparency in how data can be used, thereby protecting the rights of users and ensuring adherence to established data protection standards.

### Applicability Beyond Borders

The Data Act applies not only to entities operating within the European Union but also affects data transactions involving third countries. By establishing guidelines for data transfers, it mandates that any sharing of EU data with entities outside the Union must comply with the conditions laid out in the Act. This aspect underscores the EU's commitment to maintaining high data protection standards even in cross-border scenarios.

### Conclusion

The Data Act represents a pivotal piece of legislation in the EU's ongoing effort to enhance data accessibility while safeguarding individual rights. Its extensive applicability ensures that both personal and non-personal data are managed within a transparent framework, promoting innovation and facilitating a robust data economy. The focus on fairness, regulatory compliance, and user empowerment positions the Data Act as a crucial instrument in the contemporary data landscape. Through its provisions, it aims to reshape how data is shared, handled, and utilized across various sectors, reinforcing the EU’s commitment to data protection and privacy.

This Regulation does not prevent users, in the case of business-to-business relations, from making data available to third parties or data holders under any lawful contractual term, including by agreeing to limit or restrict further sharing of such data, or from being compensated proportionately, for example in exchange for waiving their right to use or share such data. While the notion of ‘data holder’ generally does not include public sector bodies, it may include public undertakings.

(26)

To foster the emergence of liquid, fair and efficient markets for non-personal data, users of connected products should be able to share data with others, including for commercial purposes, with minimal legal and technical effort. It is currently often difficult for businesses to justify the personnel or computing costs that are necessary for preparing non-personal datasets or data products and to offer them to potential counterparties via data intermediation services, including data marketplaces. A substantial hurdle to the sharing of non-personal data by businesses therefore results from the lack of predictability of economic returns from investing in the curation and making available of datasets or data products. In order to allow for the emergence of liquid, fair and efficient markets for non-personal data in the Union, the party that has the right to offer such data on a market must be clarified. Users should therefore have the right to share non-personal data with data recipients for commercial and non-commercial purposes. Such data sharing could be performed directly by the user, upon the request of the user via a data holder, or through data intermediation services. Data intermediation services, as regulated by Regulation (EU) 2022/868 of the European Parliament and of the Council

Where data are excluded from a data holder’s obligation to make them available to users or third parties, the scope of such data could be specified in the contract between the user and the data holder for the provision of a related service so that users can easily determine which data are available to them for sharing with data recipients or third parties. Data holders should not make available non-personal product data to third parties for commercial or non-commercial purposes other than the fulfilment of their contract with the user, without prejudice to legal requirements pursuant to Union or national law for a data holder to make data available. Where relevant, data holders should contractually bind third parties not to further share data received from them.

(27)

In sectors characterised by the concentration of a small number of manufacturers supplying connected products to end users, there may only be limited options available to users for the access to and the use and sharing of data. In such circumstances, contracts may be insufficient to achieve the objective of user empowerment, making it difficult for users to obtain value from the data generated by the connected product they purchase, rent or lease. Consequently, there is limited potential for innovative smaller businesses to offer data-based solutions in a competitive manner and for a diverse data economy in the Union. This Regulation should therefore build on recent developments in specific sectors, such as the Code of Conduct on agricultural data sharing by contract. Union or national law may be adopted to address sector-specific needs and objectives. Furthermore, data holders should not use any readily available data that is non-personal data in order to derive insights about the economic situation of the user or its assets or production methods or about such use by the user in any other manner that could undermine the commercial position of that user on the markets in which it is active. This could include using knowledge about the overall performance of a business or a farm in contractual negotiations with the user on the potential acquisition of the user’s products or agricultural produce to the user’s detriment, or using such information to feed into larger databases on certain markets in the aggregate, for example databases on crop yields for the upcoming harvesting season, as such use could affect the user negatively in an indirect manner. The user should be given the necessary technical interface to manage permissions, preferably with granular permission options such as ‘allow once’ or ‘allow while using this app or service’, including the option to withdraw such permissions.

For the purposes of this Regulation, unfair contractual terms unilaterally imposed on an enterprise should not be binding on that enterprise.

The user should be free to use the data for any lawful purpose. entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.

They are legally entitled to grant access to or share the data they hold, including data generated from connected products or services, making them pivotal in data management. entity: "REGULATION" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "The Regulation sets out the legal framework for the processing and protection of personal data within the European Union."<SEP>REGULATION refers to a comprehensive legal framework established within the European Union to govern the use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and manage the handling, sharing, and processing of data, with a strong emphasis on the protection of individuals' rights. It defines rules and directives that classify AI applications, particularly distinguishing high-risk AI systems and ensuring compliance with fundamental rights.

One key aspect of the REGULATION is its determination of the responsibilities and obligations of providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, as well as those associated with general-purpose AI models. It sets forth guidelines for the classification and assessment of these AI systems, requiring compliance with safety standards and prohibiting manipulative practices, especially in contexts involving biometric data. Additionally, the REGULATION outlines rules to ensure non-discriminatory application and protection of individuals' rights across the Union.

The REGULATION also establishes mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement of AI systems, detailing the functioning of supportive bodies such as advisory forums and scientific panels. It specifies the legal framework for the management of biometric identification systems, including their usage and implications for privacy. The REGULATION encompasses a range of aspects including standardization processes, provisions for interoperability, and the roles and responsibilities of data holders and users of connected products.

Moreover, it aims to facilitate smooth transitions between data processing services, allowing users to efficiently transfer their data and digital assets while ensuring that data access and usage are governed by consent or legitimate interest. It specifies the obligations of data holders and includes provisions for resolving disputes related to data handling, ensuring fairness in contractual arrangements. 

Overall, the REGULATION not only serves to protect individuals' rights—granting them access, rectification, and erasure of their personal data—but also demands consistency in the enforcement of data protection laws across Member States. By establishing these comprehensive guidelines and frameworks, the REGULATION promotes effective data management and enhances trust and security in data processing practices within the European Union.

question: How should connected products and related services be designed and manufactured/provided?
ground_truth: As per Article 3(1), both connected products and related services have to be designed and manufactured/provided in a way which ensures that product data and related service data, including product metadata, are: by default, easily, securely, free of charge, in a comprehensive, structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and directly accessible to the user, where relevant and technically feasible.
answer:
### Design and Manufacture of Connected Products

When designing and manufacturing connected products, several critical factors must be taken into consideration to ensure efficiency, compliance, and user satisfaction. Connected products are devices that can communicate data over the internet, generating insights based on user interactions. Therefore, manufacturers need to prioritize certain aspects in their design and production processes.

1. **User-Centric Design**: It is essential to adopt a user-centric approach, considering the end-users' needs throughout the product design process. This includes creating intuitive user interfaces that make it easy for users to interact with the product. Engaging users in the feedback loop can also help tailor the product to meet their preferences and habits.

2. **Data Generation and Communication**: Connected products must be equipped with the necessary sensors and connectivity capabilities to collect and transmit data effectively. This involves integrating appropriate hardware and software that enable real-time data sharing, allowing users to derive actionable insights from the information generated.

3. **Robustness and Security**: Ensuring the security of the data transmitted and the integrity of the product itself is crucial. Manufacturers should implement security measures that protect against unauthorized access and data breaches. This includes employing encryption techniques and following industry-standard protocols to safeguard user data.

4. **Compliance with Regulations**: Adherence to relevant regulations, such as the Data Act and Union Law focusing on data protection and privacy, is paramount. Manufacturers must ensure that their products are compliant with these legal frameworks, especially when handling personal data. This includes implementing technical and organizational measures to protect user privacy and securing data accessibility according to user rights defined under regulations.

5. **Post-Market Monitoring**: The regulation outlines requirements for post-market monitoring of connected products. Manufacturers should establish mechanisms to review performance and gather user experience data after product release. This helps in gaining insights for ongoing improvements and compliance with safety standards.

### Provision of Related Services

Connected products are often accompanied by related services that enhance their usability and functionality. These services can range from technical support to maintenance and aftermarket services. Here’s how related services should be provided:

1. **Integration with Connected Products**: Related services must be designed to seamlessly integrate with connected products. This is crucial for enhancing the overall user experience and providing additional functionalities that can leverage the data generated by the products. 

2. **Accessibility and Usability**: Related services should be easily accessible to users, enabling them to maximize the benefits from their connected products. Clear communication regarding service features, availability, and benefits can enhance user engagement.

3. **Technical Support**: Providing robust technical support during the product lifecycle is essential. Manufacturers and service providers should ensure that users have access to assistance when needed, helping them troubleshoot issues and optimizing product performance.

4. **Maintenance and Upgrades**: After the sale, related services should include options for regular maintenance and updates to the connected products. This helps prolong the life of the devices and ensures they remain up-to-date with the latest security standards and functionalities.

5. **Responsible Data Management**: When providing related services, organizations must adhere to data-sharing regulations. This includes transparent practices related to how user data is used, shared, and protected during service delivery. Clear policies regarding data access rights can foster trust with the users.

### Conclusion

In summary, the design and provision of connected products and their related services require a comprehensive approach that emphasizes user needs, regulatory compliance, and robust security measures. By focusing on these elements, manufacturers and service providers can deliver high-quality connected products that not only meet market demands but also prioritize user protection and satisfaction.

question: What information is the seller, renter or lessor, which might be the manufacturer, of a connected product obliged to provide to the user before the conclusion of a contract for the purchase, rent or lease of such product?
ground_truth: As per Article 3(2), the following data have to be communicated to the user in a clear and comprehensible manner: (a) The type, format and estimated volume of product data capable of being generated by the connected product; (b) The possibility for the connected product to generate data continuously and in real-time; (c) The possibility for the connected product to store data on-device or on a remote server, and the intended duration of retention of such data; (d) The way in which the user can access, retrieve and erase the data; (e) The technical means, the terms of use, and quality of service of such data.
answer:
### Obligations of Sellers, Renters, or Lessors of Connected Products

When entering into a contract for the purchase, rent, or lease of a connected product, the seller, renter, or lessor—who may also be the manufacturer—has specific obligations to meet in terms of transparency and information disclosure. This is particularly crucial given that connected products are designed to generate and share data, which raises concerns about data access and user rights.

#### Information Requirements Prior to Contract Conclusion

Before finalizing any agreement, the seller or manufacturer is obligated to provide the user with clear, comprehensible information regarding the following aspects:

1. **Product Data Generation**:
   - Information detailing the type, format, and estimated volume of the data the connected product is capable of generating. This could include specifics about how data is collected, what kind of data will be produced (e.g., user behavior, operational efficiencies), and potential uses for the generated data.

2. **Data Access and Usage Rights**:
   - Clear explanations about how the data may be stored, retrieved, or accessed. This also encompasses the terms of use for the data generated by the connected product, including any rights the user has to access and control their data.

3. **Data Handling Practices**:
   - A comprehensive outline of the manufacturer's data handling practices is also mandated. This includes information about the privacy measures in place to protect personal data, how data will be managed, including storage and processing guidelines, and any third parties who may have access to this data.

4. **Transparency of Terms**:
   - The obligation includes providing insights into any contractual terms that govern the use, sharing, or re-use of the data generated by the connected product. This ensures that the user is aware of their rights and the potential restrictions placed upon them by the contract.

5. **Potential Changes in Data Policy**:
   - In case of any anticipated changes in how data is collected, used, or processed during the lifetime of the connected product or service, the seller should disclose these details to the user beforehand. This is relevant for maintaining informed consent throughout the product lifecycle.

#### Importance of Compliance

These obligations are not just formalities; they are integral to user empowerment and right protection in the context of data generated by connected products. Transparency in these areas facilitates a better understanding of the product's functionality and the implications of data usage for users. Furthermore, it emphasizes the responsibility of providers to adhere to ethical standards of data management and protection as outlined in relevant regulations, thereby fostering trust and security in the marketplace.

#### Conclusion

In summary, the seller, renter, or lessor of a connected product has a crucial role in ensuring users are well-informed about the data dynamics associated with their product. This foundational information is aimed at enhancing users' rights, enabling them to make informed decisions, and fostering a fair and transparent operation within the realm of connected technology.

entity: "UNION LAW" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "Union Law" encompasses a comprehensive framework of regulations and directives established by the European Union (EU), focusing primarily on data protection, individual rights regarding personal data, and the processing obligations of member states. This body of law regulates how personal and non-personal data can be handled, ensuring conformity and protection across the EU.

Specifically, Union Law provides the legal basis required for processing personal data, governing the operations of supervisory authorities in alignment with broader European laws. It includes various regulations applicable throughout member states, particularly focusing on public access to personal data and legal obligations associated with data handling.

In addition to data protection, Union Law also extends to legal frameworks concerning artificial intelligence (AI). It establishes standards for the deployment and oversight of high-risk AI systems, promoting compliance, safety, and consumer protection. This body of law influences obligations for AI model providers and sets additional requirements for systems classified as high-risk, ensuring that they adhere to principles of fundamental rights protection and non-discrimination.

Moreover, Union Law aims to maintain legal consistency across member states in various aspects, including consumer protection, competition law, and data sharing practices. It represents the collective legal standards and regulations that guide the interaction between member states and the EU itself, fostering an environment where public interests and fundamental rights are duly protected.
entity: "DATA HOLDERS" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Data Holders" refer to individuals or entities that possess, control, or manage data, with the capacity to make that data available for processing. They may hold both personal and non-personal data, and their activities often comply with various regulations regarding data protection and sharing. 

Data Holders can share non-personal data under the principles of Data Altruism, aimed at achieving broader societal benefits. This sharing occurs with explicit consent from the Data Holders themselves, who grant permission for data processing by Data Altruism Organisations. In addition, these entities have specific rights over the data they hold, including the management of its use and protection.

The responsibilities of Data Holders include ensuring compliance with legal obligations when accessing, sharing, or exchanging data. Under new regulatory frameworks, they are mandated to share data with designated recipients. Furthermore, Data Holders are accountable for adhering to specific conditions set forth by law regarding access and usage, often involving the need to safeguard their interests and potentially receive compensation upon data sharing.

They may also be subject to requests for data access from public sector bodies or other authorities, highlighting their role in data transparency and the facilitation of data exchanges within the community, which may encompass both private and public sector organizations.

question: What information is the provider of a related service obliged to provide to the user of such service before the conclusion of a contract for the provision of such service?
ground_truth: As per Article 3(3), the following data have to be communicated to the user in a clear and comprehensible manner: (a) The nature, estimated volume and collection frequency of product data and the arrangements for access/retrieval and storage/retention; (b) The nature, estimated volume of related service data and the arrangements for access/retrieval and storage/retention; (c) The possibility for the data holder to use readily available data itself, the use purposes, and the data holder's intention of allowing third parties to use the data; (d) The identity of the data holder; (e) The means of communication for contacting the data holder; (f) The way the user can request data sharing with third parties and end data sharing; (g) The user's right to lodge a complaint pursuant to Article 37; (h) Whether the data holder holds trade secrets; (i) The duration of the contract. There is an exception for micro-enterprises according to Article 7(1) from information duties.

### Provider Obligations Regarding Related Services

When a provider of a related service engages with a user, there are specific obligations they must fulfill concerning the information provided prior to concluding a contract for the service. These obligations ensure that users are adequately informed about data handling practices associated with the service and their rights regarding data access and usage.

#### Information Disclosure Requirements

1. **Data Handling Practices**: The provider is obligated to disclose how the data will be managed, including the types of data collected, the purposes of processing, and how long the data will be retained. This transparency is essential to foster trust and ensure users are aware of how their personal data will be utilized and safeguarded.

2. **User Rights**: Users should be informed about their rights regarding data access, modification, and deletion. This includes their entitlements to retrieve their data, request corrections, or ask for the deletion of their personal information under applicable data protection regulations.

3. **Conditions of Service**: The provider must also outline the terms and conditions of service use. This encompasses any limitations on liability, data access rights, and obligations regarding confidentiality and security measures in place to protect user data from unauthorized access.

4. **Contractual Terms**: Clear articulation of the contractual terms is required. This includes specifying any fees, responsibilities, and obligations for both parties regarding data sharing and compliance with relevant regulations.

5. **Right to Withdraw Consent**: Users must be informed of their right to withdraw consent at any point, allowing them to reclaim control over their personal data if they decide they no longer wish to continue with the service.

#### Importance of Compliance

These information requirements serve not only to protect users but also to align with legal standards set forth in regulations such as Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (the General Data Protection Regulation or GDPR) and subsequent EU regulations that govern data protection and privacy. Ensuring compliance with these obligations is critical for providers to mitigate legal risks and enhance user trust in their services.

### Conclusion

In summary, the obligations of a provider of a related service to disclose information to users are multifaceted, emphasizing transparency, user rights, and legal compliance. This not only safeguards users' interests but also contributes to a more accountable and trustworthy business ecosystem in the context of data processing and service provision.
