Gradual withdrawal of switching charges

1.   From 12 January 2027, providers of data processing services shall not impose any switching charges on the customer for the switching process.

2.   From 11 January 2024 to 12 January 2027, providers of data processing services may impose reduced switching charges on the customer for the switching process.

3.   The reduced switching charges referred to in paragraph 2 shall not exceed the costs incurred by the provider of data processing services that are directly linked to the switching process concerned.

4.   Before entering into a contract with a customer, providers of data processing services shall provide the prospective customer with clear information on the standard service fees and early termination penalties that might be imposed, as well as on the reduced switching charges that might be imposed during the timeframe referred to in paragraph 2.

5.   Where relevant, providers of data processing services shall provide information to a customer on data processing services that involve highly complex or costly switching or for which it is impossible to switch without significant interference in the data, digital assets or service architecture.

6.   Where applicable, providers of data processing services shall make the information referred to in paragraphs 4 and 5 publicly available to customers via a dedicated section of their website or in any other easily accessible way.

Article 29

Processing under the authority of the controller or processor

Article 30

1.   Each controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative, shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility. That record shall contain all of the following information:

(a)

the name and contact details of the controller and, where applicable, the joint controller, the controller's representative and the data protection officer;

(b)

the purposes of the processing;

(c)

a description of the categories of data subjects and of the categories of personal data;

(d)

the categories of recipients to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed including recipients in third countries or international organisations;

(e)

where applicable, transfers of personal data to a third country or an international organisation, including the identification of that third country or international organisation and, in the case of transfers referred to in the second subparagraph of Article 49(1), the documentation of suitable safeguards;

where possible, the envisaged time limits for erasure of the different categories of data;

(g)

where possible, a general description of the technical and organisational security measures referred to in Article 32(1).

2.   Each processor and, where applicable, the processor's representative shall maintain a record of all categories of processing activities carried out on behalf of a controller, containing:

(a)

the name and contact details of the processor or processors and of each controller on behalf of which the processor is acting, and, where applicable, of the controller's or the processor's representative, and the data protection officer;

(b)

the categories of processing carried out on behalf of each controller;

(c)

where applicable, transfers of personal data to a third country or an international organisation, including the identification of that third country or international organisation and, in the case of transfers referred to in the second subparagraph of Article 49(1), the documentation of suitable safeguards;

(d)

where possible, a general description of the technical and organisational security measures referred to in Article 32(1).

3.   The records referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be in writing, including in electronic form.

4.   The controller or the processor and, where applicable, the controller's or the processor's representative, shall make the record available to the supervisory authority on request.

5.   The obligations referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to an enterprise or an organisation employing fewer than 250 persons unless the processing it carries out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the processing is not occasional, or the processing includes special categories of data as referred to in Article 9(1) or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10.

Article 31

Cooperation with the supervisory authority

The controller and the processor and, where applicable, their representatives, shall cooperate, on request, with the supervisory authority in the performance of its tasks.

Section 2

Article 32

1.   Taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including inter alia as appropriate:

(a)

the pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data;

(b)

the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services;

(c)

the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident;

(d)

a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of the processing.

International cooperation for the protection of personal data

In relation to third countries and international organisations, the Commission and supervisory authorities shall take appropriate steps to:

(a)

develop international cooperation mechanisms to facilitate the effective enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data;

(b)

provide international mutual assistance in the enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data, including through notification, complaint referral, investigative assistance and information exchange, subject to appropriate safeguards for the protection of personal data and other fundamental rights and freedoms;

(c)

engage relevant stakeholders in discussion and activities aimed at furthering international cooperation in the enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data;

(d)

promote the exchange and documentation of personal data protection legislation and practice, including on jurisdictional conflicts with third countries.

CHAPTER VI

Independent supervisory authorities

Section 1

Independent status

Article 51

Supervisory authority

1.   Each Member State shall provide for one or more independent public authorities to be responsible for monitoring the application of this Regulation, in order to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons in relation to processing and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the Union (‘supervisory authority’).

2.   Each supervisory authority shall contribute to the consistent application of this Regulation throughout the Union. For that purpose, the supervisory authorities shall cooperate with each other and the Commission in accordance with Chapter VII.

3.   Where more than one supervisory authority is established in a Member State, that Member State shall designate the supervisory authority which is to represent those authorities in the Board and shall set out the mechanism to ensure compliance by the other authorities with the rules relating to the consistency mechanism referred to in Article 63.

4.   Each Member State shall notify to the Commission the provisions of its law which it adopts pursuant to this Chapter, by 25 May 2018 and, without delay, any subsequent amendment affecting them.

Article 52

Independence

1.   Each supervisory authority shall act with complete independence in performing its tasks and exercising its powers in accordance with this Regulation.

2.   The member or members of each supervisory authority shall, in the performance of their tasks and exercise of their powers in accordance with this Regulation, remain free from external influence, whether direct or indirect, and shall neither seek nor take instructions from anybody.

3.   Member or members of each supervisory authority shall refrain from any action incompatible with their duties and shall not, during their term of office, engage in any incompatible occupation, whether gainful or not.

4.   Each Member State shall ensure that each supervisory authority is provided with the human, technical and financial resources, premises and infrastructure necessary for the effective performance of its tasks and exercise of its powers, including those to be carried out in the context of mutual assistance, cooperation and participation in the Board.

5.   Each Member State shall ensure that each supervisory authority chooses and has its own staff which shall be subject to the exclusive direction of the member or members of the supervisory authority concerned.

6.   Each Member State shall ensure that each supervisory authority is subject to financial control which does not affect its independence and that it has separate, public annual budgets, which may be part of the overall state or national budget.

Article 53

General conditions for the members of the supervisory authority

1.   Member States shall provide for each member of their supervisory authorities to be appointed by means of a transparent procedure by:

their parliament;

—

their government;

—

their head of State; or

—

an independent body entrusted with the appointment under Member State law.

question: When are parties joint controllers and what must their arrangement cover?
ground_truth: Parties are joint controllers when they jointly determine purposes and means of processing. This may arise where decisions are made together or are inextricably linked such that purposes and means are effectively determined jointly. Joint controllers must transparently determine their respective responsibilities, in particular regarding data subject rights and transparency obligations, by means of an arrangement under Article 26. The essence of the arrangement must be made available to data subjects. Regardless of internal allocation, data subjects may exercise their rights against any of the controllers. In practice, the decision chain must be mapped to verify controller roles, labelling by convenience must be avoided, and responsibilities for notices, rights requests, security, breaches, and regulator engagement must be documented. Liability, indemnities and insurance must be aligned accordingly, and processors must be informed of their instructing controller. The arrangement must be updated whenever purposes or means of processing evolve.
answer:
### Understanding Joint Controllers

Joint controllers are entities that collectively determine the purposes and means of processing personal data. This arrangement arises when multiple parties share responsibility for data management under applicable privacy laws, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Joint controllers may typically include various organizations or individuals that engage in collaborative data processes, such as companies working together on a joint project or organizations within a consortium.

### Conditions for Joint Control

To qualify as joint controllers, the parties involved must meet certain criteria:

1. **Determining Purposes and Means**: Each party must have a say in the intentions behind data processing. This involves making agreed-upon decisions about why and how data will be processed.

2. **Shared Responsibilities**: The entities must share the legal obligations and responsibilities set forth by data protection regulations. This includes liability for ensuring compliance with data protection standards, safeguarding data rights, and addressing any concerns regarding data management.

### Required Arrangements

The arrangement between joint controllers should include specific elements to ensure legal compliance and operational clarity:

1. **Transparent Arrangement**: The joint controllers must define their roles and responsibilities transparently, often articulated in a formal agreement. This agreement should detail how they will jointly manage data and protect the data subjects’ rights.

2. **Information Provided to Data Subjects**: Joint controllers are responsible for ensuring that data subjects are informed about the processing of their data, including what information is shared, with whom, and the purposes of the processing.

3. **Rights Protection**: The arrangement must cover the protections and rights of the data subjects, including their right to access, rectify, and erase their personal data. The parties should specify how these rights can be exercised by data subjects.

4. **Designated Contact Point**: It is advisable for the joint controllers to designate a point of contact for data subjects to facilitate communication and inquiries related to their personal data processing.

5. **Compliance with Legal Obligations**: The agreement must outline how each controller will handle compliance with relevant regulations, emphasizing their collective adherence to the legal framework governing personal data processing.

### Conclusion

Joint controllers play a critical role in the data processing ecosystem by fostering collaboration while adhering to legal and ethical standards. Their arrangement must be clear and thorough to ensure compliance with data protection laws and to uphold the rights of data subjects effectively. By establishing solid partnerships and agreements, joint controllers can navigate the complexities of data management with greater confidence and responsibility.

The interests and fundamental rights of the data subject could in particular override the interest of the data controller where personal data are processed in circumstances where data subjects do not reasonably expect further processing. Given that it is for the legislator to provide by law for the legal basis for public authorities to process personal data, that legal basis should not apply to the processing by public authorities in the performance of their tasks. The processing of personal data strictly necessary for the purposes of preventing fraud also constitutes a legitimate interest of the data controller concerned. The processing of personal data for direct marketing purposes may be regarded as carried out for a legitimate interest.

In situations of exceptional need, it may be necessary for public sector bodies, the Commission, the European Central Bank or Union bodies to use in the performance of their statutory duties in the public interest existing data, including, where relevant, accompanying metadata, to respond to public emergencies or in other exceptional cases. Exceptional needs are circumstances which are unforeseeable and limited in time, in contrast to other circumstances which might be planned, scheduled, periodic or frequent. While the notion of ‘data holder’ does not, generally, include public sector bodies, it may include public undertakings. Research-performing organisations and research-funding organisations could also be organised as public sector bodies or bodies governed by public law. To limit the burden on businesses, microenterprises and small enterprises should only be under the obligation to provide data to public sector bodies, the Commission, the European Central Bank or Union bodies in situations of exceptional need where such data is required to respond to a public emergency and the public sector body, the Commission, the European Central Bank or the Union body is unable to obtain such data by alternative means in a timely and effective manner under equivalent conditions.

(64)

In the case of public emergencies, such as public health emergencies, emergencies resulting from natural disasters including those aggravated by climate change and environmental degradation, as well as human-induced major disasters, such as major cybersecurity incidents, the public interest resulting from the use of the data will outweigh the interests of the data holders to dispose freely of the data they hold. In such a case, data holders should be placed under an obligation to make the data available to public sector bodies, the Commission, the European Central Bank or Union bodies upon their request. The existence of a public emergency should be determined or declared in accordance with Union or national law and based on the relevant procedures, including those of the relevant international organisations. In such cases, the public sector body should demonstrate that the data in scope of the request could not otherwise be obtained in a timely and effective manner and under equivalent conditions, for instance by way of the voluntary provision of data by another enterprise or the consultation of a public database.

(65)

An exceptional need may also arise from non-emergency situations. In such cases, a public sector body, the Commission, the European Central Bank or a Union body should be allowed to request only non-personal data. The public sector body should demonstrate that the data are necessary for the fulfilment of a specific task carried out in the public interest that has been explicitly provided for by law, such as the production of official statistics or the mitigation of or recovery from a public emergency. In addition, such a request can be made only when the public sector body, the Commission, the European Central Bank or a Union body has identified specific data that could not otherwise be obtained in a timely and effective manner and under equivalent conditions and only if it has exhausted all other means at its disposal to obtain such data, such as obtaining the data through voluntary agreements, including purchasing of non-personal data on the market by offering market rates, or by relying on existing obligations to make data available or the adoption of new legislative measures which could guarantee the timely availability of data. The conditions and principles governing requests, such as those related to purpose limitation, proportionality, transparency and time limitation, should also apply. In cases of requests for data necessary for the production of official statistics, the requesting public sector body should also demonstrate whether the national law allows it to purchase non-personal data on the market.

entity: "PRIVATE PARTIES" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Private Parties refer to individuals or organizations that are subject to legal actions for violations of data protection rules as laid out in the regulation."
entity: "DATA HOLDERS" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Data Holders" refer to individuals or entities that possess, control, or manage data, with the capacity to make that data available for processing. They may hold both personal and non-personal data, and their activities often comply with various regulations regarding data protection and sharing. 

Data Holders can share non-personal data under the principles of Data Altruism, aimed at achieving broader societal benefits. This sharing occurs with explicit consent from the Data Holders themselves, who grant permission for data processing by Data Altruism Organisations. In addition, these entities have specific rights over the data they hold, including the management of its use and protection.

The responsibilities of Data Holders include ensuring compliance with legal obligations when accessing, sharing, or exchanging data. Under new regulatory frameworks, they are mandated to share data with designated recipients. Furthermore, Data Holders are accountable for adhering to specific conditions set forth by law regarding access and usage, often involving the need to safeguard their interests and potentially receive compensation upon data sharing.

They may also be subject to requests for data access from public sector bodies or other authorities, highlighting their role in data transparency and the facilitation of data exchanges within the community, which may encompass both private and public sector organizations.

question: What are the mandatory processor obligations and what should a data processing agreement (DPA) include?
ground_truth: Processors must act only on documented instructions and are required to implement appropriate security measures, ensure confidentiality, keep records, assist with data subject rights and DPIAs, notify breaches to the controller without undue delay, and allow for audits and inspections. The controller-processor contract (DPA) must contain the clauses specified in Article 28(3): subject matter and duration of the processing, nature and purpose, type of personal data and categories of data subjects, obligations and rights of the controller; processing only on documented instructions; confidentiality; security measures; conditions for engaging a sub-processor; assistance with data subject rights and DPIAs; deletion or return upon termination of the contract; information necessary to demonstrate compliance; and audit support. Vague language should be avoided - security baselines, breach timelines, sub processor notification, and cross border transfer mechanisms must be clearly defined. Prompt disclosure of incidents and material changes must be required, and all obligations must flow down to sub processors. A vendor assurance programme (including questionnaires, certificates, and audits) must be maintained to verify ongoing compliance.
answer:
### Understanding Processor Obligations and Data Processing Agreements

In the context of data protection regulations, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), processors play a critical role in the handling of personal data. Processes are entities that process personal data on behalf of a controller and have specific legal obligations to fulfill to ensure compliance with data protection laws. Understanding these obligations is essential for maintaining data security and protecting the rights of data subjects.

#### Mandatory Obligations of Processors

Processors must adhere to several legal obligations as mandated by data protection regulations, which include:

1. **Processing Only on Instructions**: Processors are required to process personal data solely on the documented instructions of the controller. This obligation ensures that data is processed according to the controller's predefined guidelines and respects the legal parameters governing data handling.

2. **Confidentiality**: Processors must ensure that personnel involved in processing personal data are bound by confidentiality. This reinforces the need to maintain the integrity and confidentiality of the data being processed.

3. **Security Measures**: Processors are obligated to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, which includes protecting against unauthorized access or disclosure, accidental loss, or destruction of personal data.

4. **Data Breach Notification**: Should a data breach occur, the processor is required to notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of it. This allows the controller to take necessary steps to mitigate any fallout and fulfill obligations like informing supervisory authorities and affected data subjects.

5. **Sub-Processor Engagement**: If the processor intends to engage another processor (sub-processor) for processing activities, they must obtain prior specific or general written authorization from the controller. The same data protection obligations must be passed on to the sub-processor to ensure consistent standards of data protection.

6. **Assisting the Controller**: Processors must assist controllers in ensuring compliance with obligations related to the rights of data subjects, including data access, rectification, erasure, and data portability.

7. **Ending Processing**: Upon termination of the processing services or at the controller’s request, processors are required to delete or return all personal data as per the contractual terms, ensuring that data retention policies are adhered to.

#### Key Elements of a Data Processing Agreement (DPA)

A Data Processing Agreement (DPA) serves as a binding contract between the data controller and processor, outlining the specifics of data processing and both parties' obligations. A well-structured DPA should include the following essential elements:

1. **Purpose and Scope of Processing**: Clearly define the nature and purpose of the data processing operations to ensure alignment on expected outcomes and compliance needs.

2. **Types of Personal Data**: Specify the categories of personal data being processed, including potentially special categories of data, and clarify any limitations on data use.

3. **Duration of Processing**: Outline the time frame during which processing will occur, including conditions for termination and handling of data post-processing.

4. **Obligations and Rights of the Parties**: Detail the responsibilities of both the controller and processor, including security requirements, compliance duties, and confidentiality obligations.

5. **Security Measures**: Incorporate provisions that specify the security measures the processor must implement to safeguard the data being processed.

6. **Sub-Processor Clauses**: Establish terms for engaging sub-processors, including requirements for obtaining the controller’s authorization and ensuring that sub-processors provide adequate data protection guarantees.

7. **Breach Notification Protocol**: Include procedures for reporting data breaches to the controller efficiently, ensuring that all legal obligations can be met promptly.

8. **Data Subject Rights**: Outline the process through which data subjects can exercise their rights in compliance with applicable regulations, highlighting the processor’s role in assisting the controller in these matters.

9. **Termination and Return of Data**: Specify the mechanism for the return or deletion of personal data upon the termination of the DPA or at the request of the controller.

In summary, the processor's obligations are crucial for ensuring that personal data is handled in a secure and compliant manner. A comprehensive Data Processing Agreement is vital to ensuring that both controllers and processors understand their roles and responsibilities under data protection regulations, thereby enhancing the protection of individuals’ personal data.

While the notion of ‘data holder’ generally does not include public sector bodies, it may include public undertakings.

(26)

To foster the emergence of liquid, fair and efficient markets for non-personal data, users of connected products should be able to share data with others, including for commercial purposes, with minimal legal and technical effort. It is currently often difficult for businesses to justify the personnel or computing costs that are necessary for preparing non-personal datasets or data products and to offer them to potential counterparties via data intermediation services, including data marketplaces. A substantial hurdle to the sharing of non-personal data by businesses therefore results from the lack of predictability of economic returns from investing in the curation and making available of datasets or data products. In order to allow for the emergence of liquid, fair and efficient markets for non-personal data in the Union, the party that has the right to offer such data on a market must be clarified. Users should therefore have the right to share non-personal data with data recipients for commercial and non-commercial purposes. Such data sharing could be performed directly by the user, upon the request of the user via a data holder, or through data intermediation services. Data intermediation services, as regulated by Regulation (EU) 2022/868 of the European Parliament and of the Council

22
)
 could facilitate a data economy by establishing commercial relationships between users, data recipients and third parties and may support users in exercising their right to use data, such as ensuring the anonymisation of personal data or aggregation of access to data from multiple individual users. Where data are excluded from a data holder’s obligation to make them available to users or third parties, the scope of such data could be specified in the contract between the user and the data holder for the provision of a related service so that users can easily determine which data are available to them for sharing with data recipients or third parties. Data holders should not make available non-personal product data to third parties for commercial or non-commercial purposes other than the fulfilment of their contract with the user, without prejudice to legal requirements pursuant to Union or national law for a data holder to make data available. Where relevant, data holders should contractually bind third parties not to further share data received from them.

(27)

In sectors characterised by the concentration of a small number of manufacturers supplying connected products to end users, there may only be limited options available to users for the access to and the use and sharing of data. In such circumstances, contracts may be insufficient to achieve the objective of user empowerment, making it difficult for users to obtain value from the data generated by the connected product they purchase, rent or lease. Consequently, there is limited potential for innovative smaller businesses to offer data-based solutions in a competitive manner and for a diverse data economy in the Union. This Regulation should therefore build on recent developments in specific sectors, such as the Code of Conduct on agricultural data sharing by contract. Union or national law may be adopted to address sector-specific needs and objectives. Furthermore, data holders should not use any readily available data that is non-personal data in order to derive insights about the economic situation of the user or its assets or production methods or about such use by the user in any other manner that could undermine the commercial position of that user on the markets in which it is active. This could include using knowledge about the overall performance of a business or a farm in contractual negotiations with the user on the potential acquisition of the user’s products or agricultural produce to the user’s detriment, or using such information to feed into larger databases on certain markets in the aggregate, for example databases on crop yields for the upcoming harvesting season, as such use could affect the user negatively in an indirect manner. The user should be given the necessary technical interface to manage permissions, preferably with granular permission options such as ‘allow once’ or ‘allow while using this app or service’, including the option to withdraw such permissions.

(28)

In contracts between a data holder and a consumer as user of a connected product or related service generating data, Union consumer law, in particular Directives 93/13/EEC and 2005/29/EC, applies to ensure that a consumer is not subject to unfair contractual terms. For the purposes of this Regulation, unfair contractual terms unilaterally imposed on an enterprise should not be binding on that enterprise.

(29)

Data holders may require appropriate user identification to verify a user’s entitlement to access the data. In the case of personal data processed by a processor on behalf of the controller, data holders should ensure that the access request is received and handled by the processor.

(30)

The user should be free to use the data for any lawful purpose. This includes providing the data the user has received while exercising its rights under this Regulation to a third party offering an aftermarket service that may be in competition with a service provided by a data holder, or to instruct the data holder to do so. question: What are the requirements for engaging a sub-processor?
ground_truth: Sub processing requires prior specific or general written authorisation from the controller. Under general authorisation models, the processor must inform the controller of intended changes, allowing the controller to object. Contracts with sub processors must impose the same data protection obligations as between controller and processor, in particular providing sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures. A current list of sub processors, including purposes, locations and transfer mechanisms, must be maintained. Due diligence and risk assessments must be conducted, covering security posture and incident history; and audit rights must flow down between processor and sub-processor. Onward transfer mechanisms must comply with Chapter V requirements (e.g. SCCs, adequacy decisions etc.). Exit plans and data return or deletion obligations must be defined. Changes must be monitored via notifications and periodic reviews, and evidence of approvals or objections must be retained. Sub processor chains should not erode accountability, as the initial controller remains responsible for selecting processors capable of compliance.
answer:
### Engaging a Sub-Processor: Requirements and Considerations

Engaging a sub-processor is a significant aspect of data processing agreements, particularly within the context of compliance with data protection regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The following outlines the essential requirements and considerations when involving sub-processors:

#### 1. **Contractual Obligations**

When engaging a sub-processor, it is crucial to have binding contractual agreements in place. The contract should clearly define the scope of the sub-processor's responsibilities, ensuring that they are aligned with the obligations set forth by the main data processor and controller. Specifically, the contract should address:

- **Data Handling and Processing Terms**: The sub-processor must adhere to the same data protection obligations as the primary processor, including requirements related to data security and confidentiality.
- **Legal Compliance**: The agreement should stipulate that the sub-processor complies with applicable data protection laws and best practices.

#### 2. **Approval and Oversight**

In most cases, the primary processor must seek prior approval from the data controller before engaging any sub-processor. The rationale behind this requirement includes:

- **Transparency**: The data controller should be informed of who is processing their data, maintaining transparency throughout the processing chain.
- **Regulatory Compliance**: Data protection authorities may require demonstration of oversight mechanisms, ensuring that sub-processors meet established compliance standards and accepted practices.

#### 3. **Specific Provisions in Contracts**

The contract with the sub-processor should contain specific provisions to protect the rights of data subjects, including:

- **Indemnity Clauses**: It's common to include liability clauses that stipulate the sub-processor's accountability for breaches that may occur while handling personal data.
- **Confidentiality Agreements**: Ensure that confidentiality is maintained by the sub-processor, protecting sensitive data from unauthorized access or disclosure.
- **Prompt Notification of Breaches**: The sub-processor must agree to promptly notify the primary processor of any data breaches or security incidents, allowing for timely response measures.

#### 4. **Continued Compliance and Audit Rights**

The primary processor ought to retain the right to audit the sub-processor's compliance with the stipulated contractual obligations. This may involve:

- **Compliance Checks**: Regular evaluations may be necessary to ensure that the sub-processor maintains adherence to the agreed-upon security measures, processing practices, and legal obligations.
- **Changes to Processing Activities**: The primary processor should be informed of any significant changes in the sub-processor's operations that may impact data privacy or security.

#### 5. **Data Transfer Considerations**

If the sub-processor is located outside the EU or this type of location presents a risk concerning data protection standards, additional safeguards are necessary:

- **Adequate Protection Mechanisms**: The engagement must comply with rules governing international data transfers, possibly involving Standard Contractual Clauses or other approved mechanisms to ensure that data protection standards are upheld.

### Conclusion

Engaging a sub-processor involves meticulous planning and stringent compliance with regulatory requirements. The main data processor must ensure that all necessary contractual safeguards are in place, maintain oversight, and facilitate open communication with the data controller. By managing these relationships appropriately, organizations can ensure that they uphold data protection standards while leveraging the services of sub-processors efficiently.

Article 11

Technical protection measures on the unauthorised use or disclosure of data

1.   A data holder may apply appropriate technical protection measures, including smart contracts and encryption, to prevent unauthorised access to data, including metadata, and to ensure compliance with Articles 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9, as well as with the agreed contractual terms for making data available. Such technical protection measures shall not discriminate between data recipients or hinder a user’s right to obtain a copy of, retrieve, use or access data, to provide data to third parties pursuant to Article 5 or any right of a third party under Union law or national legislation adopted in accordance with Union law. Users, third parties and data recipients shall not alter or remove such technical protection measures unless agreed by the data holder.

2.   In the circumstances referred to in paragraph 3, the third party or data recipient shall comply, without undue delay, with the requests of the data holder and, where applicable and where they are not the same person, the trade secret holder or the user:

(a)

to erase the data made available by the data holder and any copies thereof;

(b)

to end the production, offering or placing on the market or use of goods, derivative data or services produced on the basis of knowledge obtained through such data, or the importation, export or storage of infringing goods for those purposes, and destroy any infringing goods, where there is a serious risk that the unlawful use of those data will cause significant harm to the data holder, the trade secret holder or the user or where such a measure would not be disproportionate in light of the interests of the data holder, the trade secret holder or the user;

(c)

to inform the user of the unauthorised use or disclosure of the data and of the measures taken to put an end to the unauthorised use or disclosure of the data;

(d)

to compensate the party suffering from the misuse or disclosure of such unlawfully accessed or used data.

3.   Paragraph 2 shall apply where a third party or a data recipient has:

(a)

for the purposes of obtaining data, provided false information to a data holder, deployed deceptive or coercive means or abused gaps in the technical infrastructure of the data holder designed to protect the data;

(b)

used the data made available for unauthorised purposes, including the development of a competing connected product within the meaning of Article 6(2), point (e);

(c)

unlawfully disclosed data to another party;

(d)

not maintained the technical and organisational measures agreed pursuant to Article 5(9); or

(e)

altered or removed technical protection measures applied by the data holder pursuant to paragraph 1 of this Article without the agreement of the data holder.

4.   Paragraph 2 shall also apply where a user alters or removes technical protection measures applied by the data holder or does not maintain the technical and organisational measures taken by the user in agreement with the data holder or, where they are not the same person, the trade secrets holder, in order to preserve trade secrets, as well as in respect of any other party that receives the data from the user by means of an infringement of this Regulation.

5.   Where the data recipient infringes Article 6(2), point (a) or (b), users shall have the same rights as data holders under paragraph 2 of this Article.

Article 12

Scope of obligations for data holders obliged pursuant to Union law to make data available

1.   This Chapter shall apply where, in business-to-business relations, a data holder is obliged under Article 5 or under applicable Union law or national legislation adopted in accordance with Union law, to make data available to a data recipient.

2.   A contractual term in a data sharing agreement which, to the detriment of one party, or, where applicable, to the detriment of the user, excludes the application of this Chapter, derogates from it, or varies its effect, shall not be binding on that party.

question: When can legitimate interests be relied on and how is the LIA conducted?
ground_truth: Legitimate interests (Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR) may apply where the controller (or a third party) has a legitimate interest that is not overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject. A Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA) must be conducted: (1) Purpose test - the specific interest and its legitimacy must be identified; (2) Necessity test - the controller must assess whether processing is necessary to achieve that interest or whether less intrusive means suffice; (3) Balancing test - the controller must consider data subject expectations, relationship, the nature of data, the impact of the processing, and the safeguards in place (e.g., minimisation, opt-outs, pseudonymisation). LIA outcomes must be documented and appropriate safeguards should be implemented accordingly. Controllers should also render it easy for data subjects to exercise their right to object to the processing where applicable, particularly in the context of direct marketing. The LIA should be updated whenever there is a change in the context of the processing (e.g., new data or new recipients).
answer:
Legitimate interests refer to a lawful basis for processing personal data under data protection regulations, particularly within the context of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This basis allows organizations to process personal data when their interests or those of a third party are not overridden by the rights and freedoms of the data subjects. However, certain criteria must be met to ensure compliance with legal and ethical standards.

### When Can Legitimate Interests Be Relied On?

1. **Balancing Test**: Organizations must conduct a balancing test to evaluate whether the legitimate interests pursued through data processing outweigh the rights and interests of the data subjects. If the data subject's rights are deemed more significant, legitimate interests cannot be relied upon as a legal basis for processing their data.

2. **Nature of the Interest**: The interest must be lawful, specific, and pursued by the controller or a third party. Valid examples include processing for fraud prevention, network security, or maintaining a customer database.

3. **Reasonable Expectation**: The data subjects should have a reasonable expectation that their data would be processed in that manner, which generally is more likely to occur when the data pertains to services they already receive or interact with.

4. **Transparency**: Organizations are required to be transparent about their data processing activities under the principle of fairness. It involves informing data subjects why their data is being processed and how it will be used.

5. **No Overriding Rights**: Legitimate interests cannot be invoked if the processing would cause harm to the data subject’s rights, interests, or freedoms. Certain categories of data, such as sensitive personal data, typically require stronger grounds for processing.

### Conducting a Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA)

Conducting a Legitimate Interest Assessment is a systematic approach that organizations should adopt when determining whether legitimate interests can justify the processing of personal data. Here’s a structured method for how this assessment should be conducted:

1. **Identify the Legitimate Interest**:
   - Clearly define what the legitimate interest is and who is pursuing it (the organization or a third party).

2. **Assess Necessity**:
   - Determine whether the processing is necessary for the stated legitimate interest. Consider whether there are less intrusive means available to achieve the same goal without processing personal data.

3. **Conduct a Balancing Test**:
   - Weigh the legitimate interest against the rights and interests of the data subjects. The assessment should consider potential impacts on privacy and the likelihood of harm to the data subjects’ rights.

4. **Document the Assessment**:
   - Keep a record of the decision-making process, including the legitimate interest identified, the necessity of processing, the results of the balancing test, and any precautions taken to mitigate risks to data subjects.

5. **Review and Monitor**:
   - Regularly review the assessment to ensure that it remains valid, particularly if there are changes in the context of processing, such as updates in business practices or regulatory changes.

In summary, while legitimate interests can provide a lawful basis for processing personal data, a careful and documented assessment must be carried out to ensure it aligns with data protection regulations and respects the rights of data subjects. This ensures that organizations are compliant with legal standards while also fostering trust and transparency with their users.

The supervisory authority should have its own staff, chosen by the supervisory authority or an independent body established by Member State law, which should be subject to the exclusive direction of the member or members of the supervisory authority.

(122)

Each supervisory authority should be competent on the territory of its own Member State to exercise the powers and to perform the tasks conferred on it in accordance with this Regulation. This should cover in particular the processing in the context of the activities of an establishment of the controller or processor on the territory of its own Member State, the processing of personal data carried out by public authorities or private bodies acting in the public interest, processing affecting data subjects on its territory or processing carried out by a controller or processor not established in the Union when targeting data subjects residing on its territory. This should include handling complaints lodged by a data subject, conducting investigations on the application of this Regulation and promoting public awareness of the risks, rules, safeguards and rights in relation to the processing of personal data.

(123)

The supervisory authorities should monitor the application of the provisions pursuant to this Regulation and contribute to its consistent application throughout the Union, in order to protect natural persons in relation to the processing of their personal data and to facilitate the free flow of personal data within the internal market. For that purpose, the supervisory authorities should cooperate with each other and with the Commission, without the need for any agreement between Member States on the provision of mutual assistance or on such cooperation.

(124)

Where the processing of personal data takes place in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or a processor in the Union and the controller or processor is established in more than one Member State, or where processing taking place in the context of the activities of a single establishment of a controller or processor in the Union substantially affects or is likely to substantially affect data subjects in more than one Member State, the supervisory authority for the main establishment of the controller or processor or for the single establishment of the controller or processor should act as lead authority. It should cooperate with the other authorities concerned, because the controller or processor has an establishment on the territory of their Member State, because data subjects residing on their territory are substantially affected, or because a complaint has been lodged with them. Also where a data subject not residing in that Member State has lodged a complaint, the supervisory authority with which such complaint has been lodged should also be a supervisory authority concerned. Within its tasks to issue guidelines on any question covering the application of this Regulation, the Board should be able to issue guidelines in particular on the criteria to be taken into account in order to ascertain whether the processing in question substantially affects data subjects in more than one Member State and on what constitutes a relevant and reasoned objection.

(125)

The lead authority should be competent to adopt binding decisions regarding measures applying the powers conferred on it in accordance with this Regulation. In its capacity as lead authority, the supervisory authority should closely involve and coordinate the supervisory authorities concerned in the decision-making process. Where the decision is to reject the complaint by the data subject in whole or in part, that decision should be adopted by the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged.

(126)

The decision should be agreed jointly by the lead supervisory authority and the supervisory authorities concerned and should be directed towards the main or single establishment of the controller or processor and be binding on the controller and processor. The controller or processor should take the necessary measures to ensure compliance with this Regulation and the implementation of the decision notified by the lead supervisory authority to the main establishment of the controller or processor as regards the processing activities in the Union.

(127)

Each supervisory authority not acting as the lead supervisory authority should be competent to handle local cases where the controller or processor is established in more than one Member State, but the subject matter of the specific processing concerns only processing carried out in a single Member State and involves only data subjects in that single Member State, for example, where the subject matter concerns the processing of employees' personal data in the specific employment context of a Member State. In such cases, the supervisory authority should inform the lead supervisory authority without delay about the matter. entity: "SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY" | type: "PARTY" | description: "The Supervisory Authority is the national body responsible for overseeing compliance with data protection regulations, as referenced in the text."<SEP>The "SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY" is an independent public authority established in each Member State to oversee the enforcement and compliance with data protection laws, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its primary role involves monitoring adherence to data protection regulations, ensuring that personal data is handled appropriately, and safeguarding the rights of data subjects.

The SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY is tasked with various functions, including addressing complaints from individuals about personal data processing, conducting investigations, and enforcing compliance through decisions that may be challenged in court. It has the authority to impose administrative fines on entities that violate data protection laws. Additionally, the Supervisory Authority promotes awareness of individual rights related to personal data and facilitates cooperation among Member States in matters concerning investigations and compliance monitoring.

Furthermore, the SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY can approve codes of conduct, issue opinions, and authorize specific data processing activities, thus playing a critical role in protecting fundamental rights associated with personal data. Overall, the Supervisory Authority serves as a key regulatory body responsible for ensuring that organizations operate within the framework of established data protection laws, thereby upholding the rights of citizens regarding their personal information.
entity: "REGULATION" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "The Regulation sets out the legal framework for the processing and protection of personal data within the European Union."<SEP>REGULATION refers to a comprehensive legal framework established within the European Union to govern the use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and manage the handling, sharing, and processing of data, with a strong emphasis on the protection of individuals' rights. It defines rules and directives that classify AI applications, particularly distinguishing high-risk AI systems and ensuring compliance with fundamental rights.

One key aspect of the REGULATION is its determination of the responsibilities and obligations of providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, as well as those associated with general-purpose AI models. It sets forth guidelines for the classification and assessment of these AI systems, requiring compliance with safety standards and prohibiting manipulative practices, especially in contexts involving biometric data. Additionally, the REGULATION outlines rules to ensure non-discriminatory application and protection of individuals' rights across the Union.

The REGULATION also establishes mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement of AI systems, detailing the functioning of supportive bodies such as advisory forums and scientific panels. It specifies the legal framework for the management of biometric identification systems, including their usage and implications for privacy. The REGULATION encompasses a range of aspects including standardization processes, provisions for interoperability, and the roles and responsibilities of data holders and users of connected products.

Moreover, it aims to facilitate smooth transitions between data processing services, allowing users to efficiently transfer their data and digital assets while ensuring that data access and usage are governed by consent or legitimate interest. It specifies the obligations of data holders and includes provisions for resolving disputes related to data handling, ensuring fairness in contractual arrangements. 

Overall, the REGULATION not only serves to protect individuals' rights—granting them access, rectification, and erasure of their personal data—but also demands consistency in the enforcement of data protection laws across Member States. By establishing these comprehensive guidelines and frameworks, the REGULATION promotes effective data management and enhances trust and security in data processing practices within the European Union.

entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. question: How is the right to rectification exercised and managed?
ground_truth: Data subjects have the right to obtain without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data and to have incomplete data completed, including by means of a supplementary statement. Controllers should provide accessible channels for data subjects to request rectification. Controllers should also adopt proportionate measures to verify the identity of the data subject and assess evidence promptly. Where accuracy of the personal data is contested, processing may be restricted pending verification (as per Article 18 of the GDPR). Recipients to whom the data have been disclosed must be notified of any rectification unless such notification is impossible or entails disproportionate effort; upon request, data subject must be informed of those recipients. Audit trails of requests and outcomes must be maintained, and changes must be reflected in downstream systems and among vendors. For opinions or assessments, contextualisation rather than overwriting should be considered (e.g., adding a note). Processes must align with sector-specific obligations (e.g., credit referencing rules) and with transparency duties, including updating the privacy notice to reflect how individuals may exercise the right.

## Overview of the Right to Rectification

The **right to rectification** is one of the fundamental rights provided under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and is crucial for ensuring that individuals have control over their personal data. This right allows a data subject to request the correction of inaccurate or incomplete personal data held by a data controller. It is instrumental in safeguarding the accuracy and reliability of personal data processing, thereby enhancing the protection of individual rights.

### Key Aspects of the Right to Rectification

1. **Definition and Scope**:
   - The right to rectification allows individuals to request the correction of any inaccurate or incomplete data related to them. This can involve correcting factual errors or updating information that has changed over time.

2. **Legal Basis**:
   - Article 16 of the GDPR explicitly states that any data subject has the right to request rectification. This reinforces the obligation of data controllers to handle personal data responsibly and accurately.

3. **Request Process**:
   - Data subjects typically exercise this right by submitting a request to the data controller. This request should specify the inaccuracies and provide any supporting information required to facilitate the rectification process.

### Responsibilities of Data Controllers

Data controllers have several responsibilities when it comes to managing requests for rectification:

1. **Assessing Requests**:
   - Upon receiving a rectification request, the data controller must assess its validity. This involves verifying whether the requested information is indeed inaccurate or incomplete.

2. **Timely Response**:
   - Data controllers are required to respond to rectification requests without undue delay, typically within one month. If more time is needed, the data subject should be informed about the delay and the reasons for it.

3. **Implementation**:
   - If a request is validated, the data controller must rectify the data and notify the data subject of the correction. This may include updating internal databases as well as informing any third parties to whom the data has been disclosed, if applicable.

4. **Record Keeping**:
   - Data controllers should maintain records of rectification requests and their outcomes to ensure compliance and transparency.

### Legal Protections and Enforcement

The right to rectification is supported by legal mechanisms that empower individuals and enhance accountability for data controllers:

1. **Complaint Mechanisms**:
   - Data subjects who encounter issues with the rectification process can lodge complaints with supervisory authorities. This reinforces the compliance obligations of data controllers and provides individuals with avenues for legal redress.

2. **Judicial Remedies**:
   - Under Article 77 of the GDPR, individuals also have the right to seek judicial remedies if they believe their rights related to data processing, including rectification, have been infringed upon.

### Conclusion

In summary, the right to rectification is a vital component of data protection legislation, empowering individuals to the accurate management of their personal data. It places significant responsibilities on data controllers to ensure that personal data is processed lawfully and fairly, thereby safeguarding the fundamental rights and freedoms of data subjects. Data subjects, therefore, can actively engage in the correction of inaccuracies in their personal data, ensuring that their privacy and rights are preserved.

question: What does the right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') cover and what are its limits?
ground_truth: Individuals may obtain erasure where: data are no longer necessary for the purposes collected; consent is withdrawn and no other basis for the processing exists; the individual successfully objects to the processing; the processing is unlawful; erasure is required by EU or member state law; or data were collected in relation to information society services offered to a child. Recipients to whom the data has been disclosed must be notified of the erasure unless such notification is impossible or entails disproportionate effort. Certain limits apply: data must not be erased where processing remains necessary for exercising freedom of expression and information, for compliance with legal obligations or public interest tasks, for archiving, research or statistical purposes subject to safeguards, or for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims. Identity appropriate verification, conflict checks with legal holds, and coordinated deletion across systems, archives and vendors must be implemented. Clear erasure channels for erasure requests must be provided, and outcomes and residual data (e.g., backups, logs) must be communicated transparently.
answer:
The right to erasure, commonly known as the "right to be forgotten," is a significant provision under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) that allows individuals, referred to as data subjects, to request the deletion of their personal data under certain circumstances. This right aims to enhance individual control over personal information and ensure privacy rights are respected in today's digital environment.

### Scope of the Right to Erasure

1. **Conditions for Erasure**: Data subjects can invoke the right to erasure in various contexts, including but not limited to:
   - When personal data is no longer necessary for the purposes for which it was collected.
   - When the consent upon which the processing is based has been withdrawn, and there are no other legal grounds for processing.
   - If the data has been processed unlawfully or infringes data protection laws.
   - When a data subject objects to processing and there are no overriding legitimate grounds for processing.

2. **Applicability**: The right applies to all personal data held by controllers, and they are obliged to erase data upon request if the conditions outlined above are met. This provision is integral in reinforcing the principle that data belongs to the individual, ensuring that people have authority over how their information is handled.

### Limits to the Right to Erasure

While the right to erasure enhances personal autonomy, it is not absolute and has several essential limitations:

1. **Public Interest and Legal Obligations**: The right does not prevail in certain situations where the data processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation or for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest. For instance, data required for legal processes must be retained even if a subject requests erasure.

2. **Freedom of Expression**: There are balances to the right of erasure concerning the freedom of expression and information. In cases where the data in question contributes to public discourse, its erasure could conflict with these rights.

3. **Archival and Research Purposes**: Data controllers may retain personal data for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research, or statistical purposes provided that the processing aligns with legal frameworks and does not infringe upon individual rights.

4. **Legitimate Business Interests**: Organizations may have legitimate interests that justify the continued processing of data, and in such cases, the right to erasure may not be applied if the interest outweighs the rights of the individual.

### Conclusion

The right to erasure is pivotal in reinforcing data protection and prioritizing individuals’ privacy rights within the EU. However, its effectiveness is balanced by provisions that ensure it does not impede other essential freedoms and responsibilities. Data controllers must navigate both the requirements of GDPR and the limits imposed by this right, emphasizing the need for a careful assessment of each request within the established legal framework.

entity: "GDPR" | type: "STATUTE" | description: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a comprehensive regulation in European Union (EU) law focused on data protection and privacy. It is designed to give individuals greater control over their personal data and establishes guidelines for the collection and processing of personal information within the EU. GDPR governs how personal data is handled, sets forth the responsibilities of data controllers and processors, and addresses the transfer of personal data outside the EU.

As a crucial legal framework, GDPR replaced the earlier Directive 95/46, reflecting advancements in technology and changes in societal expectations regarding privacy. It emphasizes the rights of individuals, including their right to access their data, rectify inaccuracies, and request deletion of their information. Overall, the GDPR aims to strengthen the protection of personal data and privacy for individuals within the European Union, making it one of the most significant pieces of legislation in the realm of data protection.

It specifies the obligations of data holders and includes provisions for resolving disputes related to data handling, ensuring fairness in contractual arrangements. 

Overall, the REGULATION not only serves to protect individuals' rights—granting them access, rectification, and erasure of their personal data—but also demands consistency in the enforcement of data protection laws across Member States. By establishing these comprehensive guidelines and frameworks, the REGULATION promotes effective data management and enhances trust and security in data processing practices within the European Union.

question: What constitutes a personal data breach and when must it be notified?
ground_truth: A personal data breach is a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data. Controllers must notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. If notification occurs after 72 hours, the controller must give reasons for the delay. Where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, the controller must also communicate the breach to affected individuals without undue delay, unless an exception applies (e.g. effective subsequent measures or disproportionate effort with public notice instead). Notifications should describe the nature of the breach, the categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and records, the likely consequences of the breach, measures taken or proposed to be taken to mitigate the breach, and contact details of the DPO or point of contact. Controllers should maintain a register of personal data breaches, run tabletop exercises, and ensure that contracts with processors require notification of any personal data breaches suffered by the processor without undue delay.
answer:
### Understanding Personal Data Breaches

A **personal data breach** is defined as any security incident that results in unauthorized access to, disclosure of, or loss of personal data. Such breaches can lead to significant risks for individuals, particularly concerning their rights and freedoms. When personal data is lost or accessed without authorization, it poses not only privacy risks but also potential harm to individuals whose data may have been exposed. 

The consequences of a personal data breach can vary widely depending on the nature of the data involved and the scope of the breach. For example, breaches affecting sensitive personal information, such as health records or financial data, typically require swift and robust responses to mitigate potential harm.

### Notification Requirements

Under **Regulation (EU) 2016/679**, commonly known as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), there are clear obligations regarding the notification of personal data breaches. Specifically, when a personal data breach occurs, the responsible party, referred to as the "Controller," must notify the relevant Supervisory Authority within **72 hours** of becoming aware of the breach. This prompt notification is crucial to ensure that the oversight authorities can take necessary actions to protect the affected individuals and uphold the standards of data protection.

In addition to notifying the Supervisory Authority, the Controller must also inform the affected data subjects if the breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. This notification should clearly explain the nature of the breach, its potential consequences, and the measures that have been taken to address the breach. This transparency fosters trust and allows individuals to take protective steps regarding their personal information.

### Conclusion

In summary, a personal data breach is an incident that compromises personal data security, potentially affecting individuals significantly. The requirement to notify both the Supervisory Authority and affected data subjects reflects a commitment to transparency and accountability in data protection practices. By adhering to these obligations, organizations can better navigate the complexities of data management in today’s digital environment, ultimately protecting individuals’ rights and privacy.

entity: "MEMBER STATES" | type: "PARTY" | description: "Member States are countries that are part of the European Union and work towards consistent data protection laws."<SEP>"Member States are countries within the EU that must adhere to the GDPR and its regulations concerning data protection and transfers."<SEP>"Member States are entities that are required to take necessary measures to comply with the Commission's decision regarding data protection."<SEP>"Member States refer to the individual countries in the EU that have obligations to inform the Commission regarding data flow regulations."<SEP>"Member States refers to the countries within the European Union that are governed by GDPR regulations and their interpretations."<SEP>Member States are the individual countries that comprise the European Union (EU) and are accountable for implementing and enforcing EU regulations, including those related to data protection, artificial intelligence (AI), and other pertinent directives. These Member States are responsible for enacting national legislation that aligns with EU laws while ensuring compliance within their jurisdictions.

Specifically, Member States have a legal obligation to implement Union law, including data protection regulations, and must establish their own supervisory authorities to oversee compliance. They are tasked with certifying dispute settlement bodies, enforcing data protection measures, and designating market surveillance authorities. In matters concerning AI, Member States are required to establish regulatory frameworks that include the implementation of AI systems regulations, particularly for high-risk applications, and must facilitate the registration and use of these systems.

Member States also play a crucial role in public security, defense, and national law, which allows them to influence how regulations are applied within their borders. They are required to notify the European Commission about their compliance measures, including rules on penalties for data transfer violations and guidelines for data processing. Additionally, they participate in discussions related to AI governance and are encouraged to support solutions that yield socially and environmentally beneficial outcomes.

Overall, Member States act as national authorities responsible for ensuring adherence to EU regulations while maintaining certain legislative competencies. They collaborate on law enforcement and judicial matters, engage in international agreements concerning data transfer, and are integral to the effective governance and oversight of both data protection and emerging technologies within the EU regulatory framework.<SEP>"Member States refer to the countries that are part of the European Union and subject to its data protection regulations."
entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.

entity: "REGULATION" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "The Regulation sets out the legal framework for the processing and protection of personal data within the European Union."<SEP>REGULATION refers to a comprehensive legal framework established within the European Union to govern the use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and manage the handling, sharing, and processing of data, with a strong emphasis on the protection of individuals' rights.
